newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's modest budget aims to cool economy.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's modest budget aims to cool economy.

text.p: Indonesia's 1997/98 draft budget was a disciplined effort designed to further cool its economy with only a modest increase in expenditure in an election year, economists said on Tuesday.
Analysts were impressed by the austere budget and praised the government's prudent approach ahead of the May poll.

"It would be hard pressed to find another country that has the fiscal discipline to bring in a quite tight public sector budget in an election year," Dennis de Tray, World Bank representative in Jakarta, told Reuters.
"The government is to be congratulated. It's generally quite a sound budget," de Tray said.
Vincent Low, economist at JP Morgan in Singapore, said the budget reiterated the government's anti-inflationary stance.
"Investors look at the government from how responsible is its behaviour. They will draw the conclusion that it is a pretty responsible and sensible sounding budget," Low said.

President Suharto proposed an 11.6 percent rise in the 1997/98 budget (April-March) from 90.62 trillion rupiah ($38.4 billion) in the current 1996/97 budget, which should allow the economy to grow by 7.1 percent against 7.8 percent in 1996.
Revenues from income and value-added taxes were set to finance more than half the country's expenditure of 101.09 trillion rupiah ($42.8 billion).
Suharto recommended that routine and development expenditures increase by 10.8 and 12.8 percent, respectively, from 1996/97.
Routine expenditures are mainly spending for personnel and maintainence expenses while development expenditures are used for strategic government investments.
De Tray said there were a number of moves within the budget which were highly justified, including the increase in health and education expenditures.
He said the relative decline in spending on power and telecommunication reflected rises in private sector investment.
"Generally, the overall sector distribution of resources has moved in a direction that we find appealing," de Tray said.
Although many economists were concerned over the ballooning current account deficit, the World Bank remained confident.
"Given the tax fiscal stance and continued good management of the macroeconomy ..., we don't see any long-term problems. We believe for the next several years they are still financeable."
However, de Tray said the government should continue to make sure price distortions were removed and added that competition and transparency in the economy should be maintained.
Indonesia's current account deficit was expected to rise to $9.8 billion in 1997/98 budget from $8.823 billion in 1996/97, but it would stay at four percent of GDP.
Low said the budget reflected Indonesia's general ethos of financial and monetary prudence which had borne fruit with its declining inflation rate.
Indonesia posted inflation of 6.47 percent in calendar 1996 against 8.64 percent in 1995. The government forecast inflation to fall to six percent in 1997/98.
Low said the overheating phase experienced by the economy was already well behind it and the government's forecasts of sustainable, non-inflationary growth looked achieveable.
While the foreign exchange market has shrugged off the budget, the stock market gave it a positive response. The local bourse is up by more than two percent since Friday.
